Header: Spodoptera exempta ( syn. Agrotis exempta ) Black armyworm in English, Ntchemberezandonda in Chichewa language

Prevention: Plant early, as late-planted crops suffer severe damage from the second generation of armyworms.
Keep the field free of grassy weeds, as young grasses are food for young caterpillars.
Keep flowering broad-leaf plants around the fields as they host natural enemies of armyworm.
Monitoring: Outbreaks mostly occur after the first rains when grasses have started growing.
Look for caterpillars with velvety black shiny heads with an inverted
V-shaped mark on the head and white strips along the sides and the back.
Look for translucent caterpillars hanging on green maize/grass, which turn green after feeding.
Damaged crop is ragged, leaving only the midrib in severe cases.

Male moths caught in pheromone traps at agricultural offices and village monitoring centres (≥30/week), in the presence of green grass and rainfall (≥5mm/week), indicate a likelihood of an outbreak in an area.
Farmers should check fields and report caterpillar presence to agricultural agents.
Get forecast updates from community and government forecasters and control if caterpillars are frequently found in the field.
Direct Control: Mechanically collect and crush caterpillars from the field.
Dig a 30cm deep trench around the maize field to trap marching caterpillars and destroy them by crushing or burying.
Shallower trenches may aid pupation if mature (6th instar larvae) are buried.
Forte and others to the caterpillars.

WHO Class
U (unlikely to present acute hazard in normal use); pre- harvest interval (PHI) 3 days; restricted re-entry interval (REI) 1 day.
Toxic to predatory mites and flower bugs that prey on armyworm eggs.

II (moderately hazardous); PHI 7 days; REI 1/2 day.
